extracted.intended_audience: people who follow debates about science and medicine in the news (general public, journalists, media consumers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for members of the public and journalists on how to evaluate news reports of scientific and medical research, with emphasis on the role and limits of peer review. Advises what to look for (publication status, methods, size, replication) and what questions to ask.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review as quality indicator (validity, significance, originality, clarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review means that other scientific experts in the field check research papers for validity, significance and originality – and for clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review tells you the research has passed the scrutiny of other scientists and is considered valid, significant and original. It is a 'kind of quality mark' for science, but publication is only the first step: findings must be re-tested and judged against other work. Do not treat peer review as a guarantee; look for replication and further confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers should comment on validity (design and methodology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment on its validity – are the research results credible; are the design and methodology appropriate?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether study design, methods and analyses are appropriate to support the conclusions. For news consumers, ask about sample size, controls, statistical analysis and whether the methods suit the claim being made. Lack of methodological detail or obvious design flaws reduces credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers should judge significance of the findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge the significance - is it an important finding?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how important the result is to the field, to health/public policy, or to general knowledge. A statistically significant finding may still be of limited practical importance. Reported 'breakthroughs' should be evaluated for real-world impact and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers should determine originality and check referencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine its originality - are the results new? Does the paper refer properly to work done by others?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the finding is novel and how it fits with existing literature. Proper referencing and situating within prior work reduces the risk of overstating novelty. Beware claims presented as new when they replicate or minimally extend prior studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers should recommend publication outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Give an opinion as to whether the paper should be published, improved or rejected (usually to be submitted elsewhere).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees provide an overall judgement (publish/improve/reject) that editors use. A 'revise and resubmit' recommendation indicates concerns that authors must address; outright rejection signals more serious problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors screen papers for journal 'fit' and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal editors receive many more papers than they can publish, so they use a two-step selection process. First, they consider whether the paper is a ‘fit’ for their journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different journals have different aims: some prioritize groundbreaking work, others narrow disciplinary focus. An editor's initial screening filters out papers that don't match scope or perceived novelty before peer review. When evaluating a report, note the journal's typical content and standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on unpublished or non–peer-reviewed research
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of the research claims you read in newspapers and magazines, find on the internet, or hear on television and the radio are not published in a peer-reviewed journal. Some of this research may turn out to be good but much of it is flawed or incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unpublished research is limited: scientists cannot repeat or use it and policy decisions should not be based on it. Ask 'Is it peer reviewed? If not, why not?' Treat non–peer-reviewed claims with caution and seek corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat single papers as preliminary; look for corroborating body of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists never draw firm conclusions from just one paper or set of results. They consider the contribution it makes in the context of other work and their own experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for multiple independent studies pointing in the same direction, meta-analyses or systematic reviews. A lone study—even if peer-reviewed—rarely suffices to establish a public truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to check whether results have been peer reviewed (citation and reporting indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: The full reference to peer-reviewed papers is likely to look like this: Fellers J H and Fellers G M (1976) Tool use in a social insect and its implications for competitive interactions. Science, 192, 70-72. ... Good journalists usually indicate whether research has been published and mention the name of the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for full bibliographic citations and the journal name; search for the paper or journal online (e.g., EurekAlert links). Be aware that some unscrupulous sources mimic citation style. Check other news reports and popular science coverage to confirm publication status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conference presentations are preliminary and often unpublished
rubrics_metrics.description: Research papers presented at scientific conferences have often begun a process of peer review but are usually still unpublished and preliminary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat conference reports as early-stage findings that may change during peer review. Wait for full peer-reviewed publication before accepting conference claims as established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review has limits in detecting fraud and misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is not a fraud detection system. Referees are likely to detect some wrongdoing, such as copying someone else’s research or misrepresenting data, because they care about their subject. However, if someone deliberately sets out to falsify data, there is sometimes no way of knowing this until the paper is published and others ... scrutinise and try to repeat the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that peer review relies on expert judgement and available information; it cannot guarantee absence of fraud. Replication, data access and post-publication scrutiny are necessary complements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review is used for funding decisions as well as publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is also used to assess scientists’ applications for research funds. Funding bodies ... seek expert advice on a scientist’s proposal before agreeing to pay for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For grant proposals, peers judge which applications represent the best science and have the potential to meet the funder's objectives. Criteria overlap with publication review (validity, significance, originality) but also include feasibility and alignment with funder goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review can be slow but is necessary for important/health-related claims
rubrics_metrics.description: In our world of instant communication and 24-hour news, a deliberative process like peer review can seem frustratingly slow. ... if there is a major breakthrough the process can be completed in weeks. Furthermore, if the findings are very important – e.g. they concern public health – then it is all the more necessary to check them through peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of justifications that high-importance findings are 'too important to wait' for peer review. While some cases are expedited, independent scrutiny is particularly vital for claims affecting public health or safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical question to ask of reported research
rubrics_metrics.description: So, no matter how exciting or compelling new scientific or medical research is, you must always ask… Is it peer reviewed? If not, why not?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it is peer reviewed, look for what other scientists say about it, the size and approach of the study and whether it is part of a body of evidence pointing towards the same conclusions. Asking these questions encourages better reporting and accountability from journalists and sources.
